The numbers you wrote down last night are not a bug in your code, and understanding exactly what produces them tells you what every practical fix is doing.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Explain why the optimizer takes extreme offsetting positions in assets with similar risk profiles.
- Relate the size of those positions to the condition number of the covariance matrix, with your own numbers.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Connect the two facts: compute the eigenvalues of your covariance matrix, take the ratio of largest to smallest, and then compute the gross exposure of the tangency portfolio. Repeat with 10, 25 and 50 assets on the same sample length and plot both quantities against the number of assets.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Show the mechanism directly: take two assets with 0.98 correlation and similar volatility, give one a slightly higher estimated mean, and solve. The optimizer goes long one and short the other in enormous size because it believes the difference in means is real and the difference in risk is nearly zero. Write down the weights.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Write one paragraph connecting this to the linkage disequilibrium case: a near-singular estimated covariance inverted and multiplied by a noisy vector produces the same instability in both fields, and the fixes are the same family.
:::
:::
